Consider the following Enhanced Entity-Relationship (EER) diagram:
                                
Note: The diagram uses (min, max) cardinality notation where:
- (1,1) indicates one-to-one relationship (each entity participates exactly once)
- (1,N) or (1,*) indicates one-to-many relationship (one entity can relate to many)
- (0,1) indicates optional participation (zero or one)
- (0,N) or (0,*) indicates optional many participation (zero or many)


A university system collects comprehensive data on students, courses, instructors, and departments. The Student entity includes attributes such as StudentID, Name, DateOfBirth, and EmailAddresses, while the Course entity has CourseID, Title, Credits, and a multivalued attribute Prerequisites. The Instructor entity has attributes such as InstructorID, Name, Department. features InstructorID, Name, and DepartmentID. The Department entity has attributes such as DepartmentID, DepartmentName, Location. contains DepartmentID, DepartmentName, and a composite attribute Address comprising Street, City, and ZipCode. A relationship 'Enrolls' connects Students to Courses with the attribute EnrollmentDate. Each Course is taught by one Instructor, and each Instructor belongs to one Department. The university employs an ISA hierarchy where the entity The the entity has attributes such as theID, Name, Description. Instructor has subtypes: FullTimeInstructor and PartTimeInstructor, with specific attributes for each subtype. A Student can be related to many Courses, and a Course can be related to many Students through the 'Enrolls' relationship (Student participation is optional, Course participation is optional). A Instructor can be related to many Courses through the 'Teaches' relationship. Many Instructors can be related to one Department through the 'BelongsTo' relationship (Department participation is optional)

questions.text: A university is redesigning its database system to manage its course offerings, student registrations, and faculty assignments. The database will include tables such as Courses (course_id, course_name, credits), Students (student_id, name, major), and Faculty (faculty_id, name, department). Additionally, relations will be established between the tables to ensure data integrity and optimized queries. The database administrator is tasked with implementing necessary integrity constraints and developing a user-friendly access interface.

questions.text: Consider the following schema of a database designed for a Hospital: Patient (patientId: int, name: varchar(100), address: varchar(150), dob: date) Appointment (appointmentId: int, patientId: int, doctorId: int, appointmentDate: date, status: varchar(20)) Doctor (doctorId: int, name: varchar(100), specialty: varchar(100), phone: varchar(15)) The 'Patient' table stores information about patients including unique patient ID, name, address, and date of birth. The 'Appointment' table contains records of patient appointments with doctors, associating each appointment with a patient and a doctor, along with the appointment date and status. The 'Doctor' table retains information about doctors, including their unique ID, name, specialty, and contact number. The 'Doctor' table manages details about doctors, including unique doctor ID, name, specialization, and contact information. Fee (feeId: int, patientId: int, amount: real, paymentStatus: varchar(20)) The 'Fee' table stores fee/payment details including payable amount and payment status.
